fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The square in the sky that holds a dozen stories", "body": "John McHugh's whole case rests on four stars the Babylonians called the IKU, a sacred irrigated field that later became the Pegasus Square. He traces how that one celestial box morphs into a flying horse, into the river god Ocean who encircles the earth, into the Garden of Eden, into Noah's ark as both boat and box, and into the heavenly tablet on which Islam says the Quran is kept. Chance Garton calls it possibly the most fascinating piece of astro theology, and John admits the title of his own slide could barely hold the greatest hits."}, {"title": "Why cuneiform signs carry a hundred meanings", "body": "The engine of the argument is polysemy. John explains that cuneiform has roughly six hundred signs, and each one carries many readings, so the single sign AN can mean sky, deity, star, barley, mine, and even to impale on a stake. The Sumerians invented the script around 3000 BC, Sumerian died as a spoken tongue near 1800 BC, and the Akkadian speakers kept it alive through logograms and Sumerian Akkadian dictionaries. Chance suggests the tangle grew because scribes in different temples abbreviated the same signs differently and later generations inherited every meaning as true."}, {"title": "Wordplay treated as divine revelation", "body": "For Mesopotamian scholars, finding a pun was finding a secret. John points to the phrases amat natsirti, hidden words, and pirishtu shai ili, secrets of the gods, and to Scott Noegel's work on punning, where a name embodies the essence of its bearer. His clearest proof is Enuma Elish tablet seven, where the fifty Sumerian titles of Marduk generate all one hundred sixty three lines through wordplay, including the line about the god Nibiru crossing. He also notes that the papal office rests on a pun, since Jesus calls Peter rock and builds a church on it."}, {"title": "Homer as a Babylonian hostage", "body": "How did more than half the Mesopotamian constellations reach Greece? John rejects the polite story about traders swapping techniques in Phoenicia. Hesiod, the first Greek to mention Pegasus around 700 BC, draws his themes straight from Enuma Elish. Daniel is a hostage astrologer under Nebuchadnezzar, Zenodotus of Mallus claimed Homer was a Babylonian, and Lucian's mock interview has Homer say his name was Tigranes before captivity. Homer literally means hostage. John's theory is that a Babylonian tupsharru, taken as booty in an eighth century raid, taught the constellation writing directly to the Greeks."}, {"title": "Rock art, hierophanies and when to pray", "body": "Before the decode, John shares his other life as lead archaeologist for the Utah Cultural Astronomy Project, studying Fremont and ancestral Pueblo petroglyphs. He shows a thousand year old pictograph whose headdress lights at summer solstice, a pendant marking thirteen moons and the eighteen point six one year lunar standstill, and kivas aligned to solstice sunrises. His practical advice is to pray at sunrise, sunset and solar noon, build during a waxing moon, release during a waning one. Chance adds that Easter itself is pagan, linking the word to Ishtar, the Norse Aesir and the Etruscan Iser."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The author and Adept archaeo-astronomer John McHugh returns to InnerVerse to reveal more of the Celestial Code of scriptural miracle stories. In this episode John will take us through the innumerable iterations of a sacred square in the heavens, as it morphs through mythologies and becomes the Garden of Eden, the River Oceanus, the Ark (boat and box), and the sacred tablet of Al Qu'ran. All that and some Easter insights too!
